questions.q: How does French stress one word of a sentence?
choices: By rebuilding the sentence around it, usually with c'est ... qui / que
By saying that word louder, as in English
By moving that word to the front and changing nothing else
By repeating the word twice
questions.why: French word order carries the grammatical roles, so a word cannot simply be moved or shouted. Emphasis is a construction, which is why there are fixed frames to learn.

questions.q: Stress the subject: « Pierre a cassé le vase. »
choices: C'est Pierre qui a cassé le vase.
C'est Pierre que a cassé le vase.
C'est Pierre qu'il a cassé le vase.
Pierre c'est qui a cassé le vase.
questions.why: Pierre was the subject of casser, so the connector is qui. Qui never elides either, which rules out qu'il here.

questions.q: Stress the object. Complete: « C'est le vase ___ Pierre a cassé. »
questions.why: The choice between qui and que is decided by the role the stressed word played in the plain sentence, not by whether it is a person. The vase was the object, so que.

questions.q: Complete with the right form of avoir: « C'est toi qui ___ raison. »
questions.why: Qui passes the person straight through to the verb, so the verb conjugates for toi. C'est is a separate clause and has no say in it.

choices: C'est moi qui fais la cuisine.
C'est moi qui fait la cuisine.
C'est moi qui faire la cuisine.
C'est je qui fais la cuisine.
questions.why: The commonest error in the whole construction: the verb agrees with the stressed pronoun, never with c'est. And the pronoun in the slot is always the stressed form, so moi, not je.

questions.q: Complete with the right form of être: « C'est nous qui ___ en retard. »
questions.why: Nous takes sommes even behind c'est. Nous and vous are where the agreement is audible, so they are the forms worth drilling.

questions.q: Which is the careful written form of « they're the ones who decided »?
choices: Ce sont eux qui ont décidé.
C'est eux qui a décidé.
Ce sont eux qui a décidé.
Ce sommes eux qui ont décidé.
questions.why: Ce sont is used before a plural noun or eux / elles, and the verb after qui still conjugates for eux. Speech says c'est eux everywhere; writing does not.

questions.q: Complete: « C'est à Paris ___ il habite. »
questions.why: A place is not a subject, so the connector is que, and que elides before a vowel. Qui in the same slot would never elide.

choices: C'est de toi que je parle.
C'est toi que je parle de.
C'est toi dont je parle de.
C'est toi que je parle.
questions.why: The preposition moves into the highlighted slot with its word. French never leaves a preposition stranded at the end of a clause, however normal that is in English.

choices: Ce dont
Ce que
Ce qui
Ce quoi
questions.why: Avoir besoin takes de, and ce dont is the form that swallows that de. Look at what the verb on the left demands: subject means ce qui, direct object ce que, de means ce dont.

questions.q: Complete with one short word: « Ce dont j'ai envie, c'est ___ un week-end au calme. »
questions.why: The de that justified ce dont has to reappear on the other side of c'est, because the verb is still avoir envie de. Leaving it out is the standard slip.

choices: Je, je pense que c'est une erreur.
Moi, je pense que c'est une erreur.
Le film, je l'ai vu hier.
Je l'ai vu hier, le film.
questions.why: Dislocation puts the stressed form out front (moi, toi, lui, eux) and keeps the ordinary subject pronoun in front of the verb. The doubling is correct and extremely common; only the wrong pronoun form breaks it.

questions.q: Build the sentence: I'm the one who paid.
questions.why: Two halves: c'est moi, then qui ai payé. The auxiliary is ai and not a because it takes its person from moi.

questions.q: Build the split sentence: what I need is a coffee.
questions.why: The left half names the topic, the right half after c'est delivers the point, and the de shows up on both sides because avoir besoin de governs the whole thing.
Hearing the agreement is the point: as, not a. The verb after qui belongs to the stressed pronoun in front of it.

questions.q: Say this out loud, pausing at the comma.
questions.why: The pause is what makes a split sentence work: the left half sets up the topic, the right half lands the emphasis. Ce qui because compte needs a subject.

questions.q: Give the four ways of putting something in relief, one example each: a subject, an object or a time, a whole idea, and the spoken pattern.
a: Subject: C'est moi qui fais la cuisine, or Ce sont eux qui ont décidé in writing, with the verb agreeing with the stressed pronoun. Object or time: C'est ce livre que je veux, C'est demain que je pars, C'est à Paris qu'il habite, with any preposition travelling into the slot. Whole idea: Ce qui m'intéresse, c'est la musique / Ce que je veux, c'est partir / Ce dont j'ai besoin, c'est d'un café, choosing by what the verb on the left needs. Spoken: dislocation, Moi, je pense que non, or Le film, je l'ai vu, with the pronoun duplicated on purpose.
questions.why: The four cover almost everything you will hear. Choosing between them is a matter of the grammatical role of the thing you want to stress, and of how formal you are being.
